data.title: The case for brownfield automation
data.excerpt: New lines are photogenic. Existing lines pay the bills. Most of the industrial opportunity in the region sits inside plants that cannot stop.
data.body:
A greenfield factory can be designed as a system from the first drawing. A brownfield plant must be improved while it runs, with incomplete drawings, mixed vintages, and a team that remembers why the last project hurt.

That is exactly why brownfield work matters. The installed base produces today's revenue, and its constraints are usually well understood by the people closest to it.

Sequence around the constraint

The first question is not where to put a robot. It is which constraint, when relieved, changes the economics of the plant. That may be a manual inspection step, an unreliable transfer, or a changeover that consumes a shift.

  • Model the existing process before proposing equipment.

  • Keep a running line running; design shutdown windows as part of the plan.

  • Retain reliable legacy assets and isolate the unsafe ones.

  • Train the maintenance team before handover, not after.

Accept imperfect information

Brownfield projects rarely begin with complete documentation. The discipline is to make assumptions visible, verify them early, and design for discovery. A two-week survey that finds the hidden constraint is cheaper than a six-month build around the wrong one.

related.excerpt: A line optimised for one product is a line that punishes every product after it. Changeover is a design constraint, not an operator problem.
